topic: The Biology and Dangers of the Great Barrier Reef

text.content: Spanning a distance exceeding 2,300 kilometers off the north-eastern coastline, the vast underwater ecosystem known as the Great Barrier Reef in Australia represents one of the most significant natural formations on Earth. Observers situated in outer space are capable of viewing this massive marine structure without visual assistance. Although appearing to be composed of inanimate geological formations, the entire reef consists of living organisms.

Serving as the principal architects of this habitat, millions of microscopic, soft-bodied organisms continuously build its fundamental framework. Following the death of these individual creatures, rigid limestone skeletons remain in place. Accumulated over thousands of years, these calcium carbonate structures gradually coalesce to form the underlying matrix of the marine feature. These primary organism builders are systematically identified by marine biologists as coral polyps.

Offering essential protection and abundant nutritional resources, the habitat supports an exceptionally diverse array of marine fauna. Numerous species of aquatic life inhabit the crevices between coral formations daily. Furthermore, critical breeding and feeding grounds are provided for larger species, including marine turtles, dugongs, and predatory reef sharks. Consequently, this high concentration of biodiversity renders the environment one of the most intricate ecological systems globally.

Contrary to common perception, the vivid pigmentation observed within coral colonies does not originate from the host organism itself. Rather, microscopic algae residing within the transparent tissue of the animal produce these distinctive shades. Utilizing solar energy through photosynthesis during daylight hours, these tiny entities synthesize nutrients that are transferred to the host to sustain its survival. These photosynthetic algal symbionts are formally designated as zooxanthellae.

Driven by rising sea temperatures associated with global climate shifts, this interdependent biological relationship faces widespread disruption. Under environmental stress, the host organisms forcefully expel their resident photosynthetic algae. Deprived of these essential energy sources, the affected corals experience rapid discoloration and face potential mortality through starvation. Within ecological literature, this destructive phenomenon is formally termed coral bleaching.

stage_3_logic.instructions: Are the following statements True, False, or Not Given according to the text?

questions.prompt: The pigmentation of coral tissue is exclusively produced by the host organism.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D explicitly states that the vivid pigmentation does not originate from the host organism itself, but from microscopic algae residing within the tissue.

questions.prompt: Coral bleaching occurs exclusively when sea temperatures decrease below normal seasonal averages.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E clarifies that coral bleaching is driven by rising sea temperatures rather than falling temperatures.

questions.prompt: The Australian government has introduced legal restrictions on commercial fishing near the reef to prevent ecosystem degradation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C discusses the biodiversity of the reef, but no mention is made regarding government legislation or commercial fishing restrictions.
